title: Todoist API: Endpoints, Rate Limits and Errors (2026)
summary: Todoist API lets you automate task creation. Get API credentials, make your first request to add a task, and understand rate limits.
body_markdown:
## Todoist Automation with Activepieces


To connect Todoist to other apps without writing code, Activepieces gives you a workflow builder with 750 integrations and an MIT-licensed core, so most of your current toolchain is probably already integrated.


That covers the "first task in minutes" part of the problem and leaves the production-hardening part with you.


That distinction matters after the seven items above: a visual builder doesn't remove rate limits, ID handling or version changes. It moves where you deal with them.


### Create Todoist tasks from other apps


In Activepieces, a flow is a trigger followed by steps, and every plan, including free, allows unlimited flows.


The screenshot below shows the shape: a Typeform trigger labeled "New Submission", an AI Agent step, and an Asana action that creates a task, stacked vertically on the canvas.


Swap the Asana action for a Todoist one and you have the common pattern, a form response becoming a task.


Study the right panel, because it shows the trigger's configuration with required Connection and Form fields and an error reading "Throws an error, reconnect or refresh the page."


That message is what an expired or revoked connection looks like in practice, so someone has to own reconnecting it, or the flow stops creating tasks without anything else going wrong.


The panel also offers Generate Sample Data, Test Trigger and Use Mock Data, and mock data is useful for wiring steps together but proves nothing about how real payloads behave.


Next comes the question of what the builder can't do for you.


### Calling the Todoist API from a workflow step


When the Todoist integration lacks an action you need, an HTTP step lets you call the Todoist API directly with your own token. That's the route where the article's concerns come back to you in full.


You choose the endpoint and version, so a deprecation is your problem to notice. You store the IDs a response returns, so mapping them between steps is on you.


And if a request is rejected for exceeding limits, nothing retries it unless you build that branch.


Activepieces doesn't replace that design work. It also doesn't make Todoist's behavior its own: limits and versioning remain Todoist's rules.


What it does change is who reviews the work: flows sync to git and move from a test environment to production through Release Management, so a pinned API version or a retry branch gets reviewed like code instead of living only in a vendor's UI.


Separate projects and environments make that promotion a deliberate step rather than a stray click on publish, and MoneyGram and Moneypenny run Activepieces in production.


Activepieces' own documentation covers Git Sync and Release Management, and the Ultimate plan's feature list names both alongside custom RBAC and audit logs, in the same product whether you self-host it or use the cloud.


Before you commit, check two things on the day you read this, 2026-11-22 or later. Activepieces' pricing page lists the credit-based plans, with unlimited flows on every tier, and Todoist is one of the integrations in the catalogue.


Both can change, and neither is something this article can vouch for.
